screens.title: Duplicated Code & Extract Method
screens.narratorSegment: In this lesson we tackle duplicated code and the Extract Method refactoring. Duplicated code occurs when identical or very similar blocks of logic appear in more than one place. That repetition makes systems harder to change and easier to break. You will learn to recognize both exact and subtle duplication, why it causes maintenance cost and buggy inconsistencies, and how the Extract Method turns repeated logic into a single, named implementation. We will walk through a concrete Python example showing duplicated membership checks, extract that logic into a private helper, and then parameterize it when the behavior varies. Along the way we discuss common mistakes—extracting the wrong-sized chunk, poor names, and introducing new dependencies—and simple safety practices like extracting in small steps and running tests after each change. By the end you’ll understand how a focused Extract Method reduces code size, improves readability, and creates a single source of truth for rules. Think about a time you fixed a bug in one place and later found the same bug elsewhere; here you’ll learn the disciplined steps to prevent that repeat work.

screens.title: What is Duplicated Code?
screens.narratorSegment: Duplicated code is any place where the same or very similar code appears more than once. This includes exact clones of lines and cases where logic is the same but variable names, formatting, or minor condition differences hide the repetition. The important point is shared intent: if two blocks do the same job, they should usually be expressed once. As an example, two methods that both check membership level and apply different multipliers are likely repeated intent even if the print statements or variable names differ. A common misconception is that duplication is harmless if each copy uses different variable names; it's not. The maintenance cost comes from having multiple places to update when the rule changes. In practice, finding duplication can be straightforward—search for repeated control structures, repeated calculations, or identical setup and teardown sequences. The taught remedy is to centralize that intent using a named method. That not only removes duplication but also serves as documentation: the method name explains what the logic does. As you practice, focus on the intent behind code, not just character-level similarity. How would you refactor a repeat that only differs by a single message? Often parameterization is enough; we'll show that next.

keyIdea.title: Definition
keyIdea.text: Duplicated code means repeated intent across the codebase, not just identical characters.

content.html:
Core Concept

What is duplicated code?

Repeated logic appears as identical lines or near-duplicates that implement the same rule in multiple places.

Key signals
  • Repeated control structures like identical if/else blocks across methods.
  • Similar setup/teardown sequences in multiple functions.
  • Duplicate calculations with different names but same formula.
Concrete example
Two methods each check a customer's membership tier to decide points and discounts. Same intent, duplicate logic.
Key Takeaway

Duplication hides intent and multiplies your maintenance surface; prefer a single named implementation.

Common misconception

Different variable names or logging messages do not remove duplication if the underlying logic is the same. Treat the rule as the unit of reuse.

Check your understanding
  1. Find two small functions that repeat a calculation.
  2. Ask whether they express the same business rule.
  3. If yes, consider extraction and parameterization.
Why it matters
A single source of truth reduces risk: one change, one place to update, fewer missed fixes.

screens.title: Extract Method: The Steps
screens.narratorSegment: Extract Method is a deliberate sequence of small, test-backed steps. First, identify a coherent block of code with a single responsibility and confirm it repeats. Second, create a new method name that describes intent—if you struggle to name it, the chunk is likely doing too much. Third, move the block into the new helper and replace each original occurrence with a call. Fourth, parameterize any differing parts by adding arguments to the new method instead of letting it capture external state. Fifth, run your tests after each small change and be ready to revert if behavior changes unexpectedly. A common oversight is extracting too large a block. If a method still contains multiple responsibilities after extraction, split it further. Another mistake is forgetting to update all call sites—manually verify replacements or use automated tooling. Finally, keep the helper private if it’s internal logic. Practically, you should extract, run tests, repair failures, then extract the next small chunk. This iterative discipline keeps the system stable and makes debugging easier if something breaks. Extract Method: The Steps means identify a single responsibility, name it, extract, parameterize, and test after each step.. In practical terms, a small-steps process for safe extraction. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.text: Identify a single responsibility, name it, extract, parameterize, and test after each step.

content.html:
Process Flow

Extract Method: The Steps

1. Identify
2. Name
3. Extract
4. Parameterize
5. Test
Details & tips
  • Name the method to express the 'what' not the 'how'.
  • Pass differing values as parameters; avoid capturing distant state.
  • Extract small logical chunks and run tests after each move.
Example checklist
Confirm the block has one responsibility, can be named, and is repeated in two or more places. If so, extract.
Common mistake
Extracting a block that still does multiple things. If naming is hard, split further before extraction.
Key Takeaway

Extraction is a small, test-backed process: pick, name, extract, parameterize, and test.

content.html:
Example

Customer class — before

Original code (excerpt)
class Customer:
  def __init__(self, name, member_status, purchases):
    self.name = name
    self.member_status = member_status
    self.purchases = purchases

  def calculate_loyalty_points(self):
    if self.member_status == 'Gold':
      print(f"[{self.name}] Gold member - calculating points with bonus.")
      points = sum(self.purchases) * 0.15
    elif self.member_status == 'Silver':
      print(f"[{self.name}] Silver member - calculating points.")
      points = sum(self.purchases) * 0.10
    else:
      print(f"[{self.name}] Standard member - calculating points.")
      points = sum(self.purchases) * 0.05
    return points

  def apply_discount(self, total_amount):
    discount_rate = 0.0
    if self.member_status == 'Gold':
      print(f"[{self.name}] Gold member - applying 20% discount.")
      discount_rate = 0.20
    elif self.member_status == 'Silver':
      print(f"[{self.name}] Silver member - applying 10% discount.")
      discount_rate = 0.10
    else:
      print(f"[{self.name}] Standard member - no discount.")
      discount_rate = 0.0
    return total_amount * (1 - discount_rate)
Notes
  • The same membership checks appear in two methods.
  • Print statements differ, but the membership-to-rate mapping is duplicated.
  • If rules change, multiple places must be updated.
Misconception
Different outputs mean the logic can't be shared. In fact, shared rules can be called and the final calculation kept in each method.

screens.title: Customer Class — After Refactor
screens.narratorSegment: Here is the refactored Customer class that uses an extracted private helper to centralize the membership details. The helper returns the membership name, points multiplier, and discount rate. Both calculate_loyalty_points and apply_discount call this helper and then perform their specific calculations or prints. This eliminates duplicate conditional structures while keeping behavior unchanged. A key teaching moment is parameter selection: the helper returns shared values while each caller chooses which values to use. Another important detail is naming: the helper is named to communicate its responsibility — returning member status details. Naming matters because it documents intent and makes future changes easier. One pitfall to watch for is accidental reliance on external state; the helper should accept parameters or use only fields that make sense for its scope. After extracting, run tests or simple assertions to confirm behavior is preserved. If a test fails, revert the change and try a smaller extraction. This refactor reduces the number of places to update when the membership tiers change, making the code easier to maintain. In practical terms, extracting membership logic into a helper method. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Refactor

Customer class — after

Refactored code (excerpt)
class Customer:
  def __init__(self, name, member_status, purchases):
    self.name = name
    self.member_status = member_status
    self.purchases = purchases

  def _get_member_status_details(self):
    if self.member_status == 'Gold':
      return "Gold", 0.15, 0.20
    elif self.member_status == 'Silver':
      return "Silver", 0.10, 0.10
    else:
      return "Standard", 0.05, 0.0

  def calculate_loyalty_points(self):
    status_name, points_multiplier, _ = self._get_member_status_details()
    print(f"[{self.name}] {status_name} member - calculating points.")
    points = sum(self.purchases) * points_multiplier
    return points

  def apply_discount(self, total_amount):
    status_name, _, discount_rate = self._get_member_status_details()
    print(f"[{self.name}] {status_name} member - applying {discount_rate*100}% discount.")
    return total_amount * (1 - discount_rate)
Explanation
  • The membership-to-values mapping is in one place now.
  • Each caller requests only the value it needs, reducing duplication.
  • Changing tier multipliers or rates requires updating one method.
Pro tip
Prefix internal helpers with an underscore to indicate a private implementation detail.
Key Takeaway

A single helper reduces repetition and becomes the authoritative place for membership rules.

screens.title: Parameterization — When Behavior Varies
screens.narratorSegment: Not all duplicated code is identical. Often the shared block varies in small ways—for instance, the printed message or whether a caller needs a points multiplier or a discount rate. Parameterization is the act of identifying those varying parts and turning them into arguments for the extracted method. This keeps a single implementation while allowing flexible behavior. A concrete example: if two call sites differ only by the message context, pass a context parameter or a formatting string to the helper. A common trap is to let the helper reach into external variables instead of accepting parameters. That creates hidden dependencies and reduces reuse. Another pitfall is passing large object graphs instead of the specific values the helper needs; prefer explicit, minimal arguments. When parameterizing, choose descriptive parameter names and keep the method’s signature small. If the method needs too many parameters, the chunk may still be doing too much and should be split. Parameterization preserves the single source of truth while allowing slight differences across call sites. The learner question to consider: what would you pass if callers need different logging messages and different numeric multipliers?

keyIdea.title: Parameterization
keyIdea.text: Expose the varying parts as parameters to keep one implementation that serves multiple needs.

content.html:
Definition

Parameterize the extracted method

Give the helper the differing data as arguments, not by capturing context implicitly.

Good parameter candidates
  • Different messages or context strings.
  • Numeric multipliers, rates, or thresholds.
  • Flags that select small behavioral variants.
Anti-patterns
  • Passing entire objects when a single field suffices.
  • Not passing values and relying on global or instance state.
  • Adding many parameters instead of splitting responsibilities.
Quick example
If callers differ only in the printed phrase, pass a context string; if they differ in numeric rates, return all rates and let callers pick.
Key Takeaway

Parameterize small differences to reuse one implementation while keeping explicit, simple method signatures.

screens.title: Pitfalls When Extracting Methods
screens.narratorSegment: Extract Method is powerful but easy to misuse. First, extracting too little fails to remove duplication and leaves maintenance burden intact. Extracting too much can hide responsibilities and make the new method hard to name. If you cannot name the helper clearly, split the chunk into smaller methods. Second, poor naming is misleading: a name that describes implementation rather than intent forces future readers to inspect internals. Third, introducing new dependencies into the extracted method is a frequent error. Avoid capturing unrelated variables from the original scope; pass what you need as arguments. This prevents feature envy and makes the helper more reusable. Fourth, forgetting to update all call sites undermines the whole refactor. Use automated refactors when possible and run tests to find missed replacements. Finally, neglecting to run tests after each step is risky. If tests fail, revert the small change, diagnose the failure, and try a more incremental approach. The safe workflow is extract, test, and iterate. Keeping these pitfalls in mind will make your refactorings reliable and maintainable. content.html:
Common Mistakes

Pitfalls When Extracting Methods

Granularity errors
Extracting an incoherent chunk makes naming and testing harder. Aim for single responsibility.
Naming problems
Names should express the 'what' and the business intent, not the implementation steps.
Dependency traps
Avoid letting the helper rely on many outer variables. Prefer explicit parameters to hidden coupling.
Testing mistakes
Run tests after each extraction and revert immediately if behavior changes unexpectedly.
Check your practice

screens.title: Why Single Source of Truth Matters
screens.narratorSegment: Centralizing logic via Extract Method supports the Single Source of Truth principle: a piece of information or a business rule should exist in only one place. When you obey this principle, changes happen in one place, tests continue to pass, and you reduce the cognitive load for future maintainers. Imagine a billing rule scattered in five files. Updating that rule safely requires changing all five places and running many tests. Centralization reduces those five changes to one. A frequent misconception is that extracting into a helper moves complexity around instead of reducing it. The difference is intent and scope: a well-named helper clarifies what the rule does, while scattered copies force readers to re-derive intent each time. In larger systems, single-source helpers can also be reused by multiple modules and become the foundation for higher-level abstractions. The practical question is this: when does centralization add coupling that outweighs its benefits? Use tests, small-step refactoring, and code review to ensure the helper remains focused and loosely coupled. fullNarratorScript:
In this lesson we tackle duplicated code and the Extract Method refactoring. Duplicated code occurs when identical or very similar blocks of logic appear in more than one place. That repetition makes systems harder to change and easier to break. You will learn to recognize both exact and subtle duplication, why it causes maintenance cost and buggy inconsistencies, and how the Extract Method turns repeated logic into a single, named implementation. We will walk through a concrete Python example showing duplicated membership checks, extract that logic into a private helper, and then parameterize it when the behavior varies. Along the way we discuss common mistakes—extracting the wrong-sized chunk, poor names, and introducing new dependencies—and simple safety practices like extracting in small steps and running tests after each change. By the end you’ll understand how a focused Extract Method reduces code size, improves readability, and creates a single source of truth for rules. Think about a time you fixed a bug in one place and later found the same bug elsewhere; here you’ll learn the disciplined steps to prevent that repeat work.

By the end of these lessons you will reliably find duplicated code and understand the cost of repeated logic. First, you will recognize exact and near-duplicates that violate the DRY principle and create maintenance risk. Second, you will explain why duplication increases code size, creates inconsistent behavior when one copy is changed, and makes bug-fixing more expensive. Third, you will be able to apply the Extract Method technique: selecting a coherent block, creating a new helper, replacing the original occurrences, and running tests. Fourth, you will begin to master parameterization—how to pass varying values into an extracted method so it fits slightly different call sites. Each objective links a practical skill to why it matters, and every extraction will be practiced with tests and small, reversible steps to keep the system stable.

Beyond recognition and extraction, you will develop safe habits. First, learn to pick the right extraction size: neither a single line nor an entire unrelated feature. Second, name extracted methods clearly; a good name expresses intent and reduces mental overhead. Third, run tests after each small refactor step and be prepared to revert if behavior changes. Fourth, watch for introducing new dependencies—pass values as parameters instead of relying on distant state. These habits reduce the chance of introducing regressions and keep the codebase stable during a sequence of refactorings. We will practice these skills with a Python settings manager example and a membership helper extraction so you can see tests and small-step extraction in action. Skills & Safety Goals means refactor in small steps, use clear names, parameterize rather than capture context, and always run tests.. In practical terms, practical habits to make refactoring safe and repeatable. A simple real-world example is helpful here, because students learn best when they can connect the idea to a familiar situation. This matters because it gives the learner a clear mental model and helps them connect the concept to later examples and problems. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Duplicated code is any place where the same or very similar code appears more than once. This includes exact clones of lines and cases where logic is the same but variable names, formatting, or minor condition differences hide the repetition. The important point is shared intent: if two blocks do the same job, they should usually be expressed once. As an example, two methods that both check membership level and apply different multipliers are likely repeated intent even if the print statements or variable names differ. A common misconception is that duplication is harmless if each copy uses different variable names; it's not. The maintenance cost comes from having multiple places to update when the rule changes. In practice, finding duplication can be straightforward—search for repeated control structures, repeated calculations, or identical setup and teardown sequences. The taught remedy is to centralize that intent using a named method. That not only removes duplication but also serves as documentation: the method name explains what the logic does. As you practice, focus on the intent behind code, not just character-level similarity. How would you refactor a repeat that only differs by a single message? Often parameterization is enough; we'll show that next.

Extract Method is a deliberate sequence of small, test-backed steps. First, identify a coherent block of code with a single responsibility and confirm it repeats. Second, create a new method name that describes intent—if you struggle to name it, the chunk is likely doing too much. Third, move the block into the new helper and replace each original occurrence with a call. Fourth, parameterize any differing parts by adding arguments to the new method instead of letting it capture external state. Fifth, run your tests after each small change and be ready to revert if behavior changes unexpectedly. A common oversight is extracting too large a block. If a method still contains multiple responsibilities after extraction, split it further. Another mistake is forgetting to update all call sites—manually verify replacements or use automated tooling. Finally, keep the helper private if it’s internal logic. Practically, you should extract, run tests, repair failures, then extract the next small chunk. This iterative discipline keeps the system stable and makes debugging easier if something breaks. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. Let's step through the concrete Python example that illustrates a common duplication pattern. We have a Customer class with methods to calculate loyalty points and apply discounts. Both methods contain an identical if-elif-else block that checks the member status and sets multipliers or discount rates. The duplication shows as repeated business rules scattered in separate methods. A typical misconception is to leave these as-is because the outputs differ: one computes points and the other computes a discount. But the membership tier logic is shared intent and should be centralized. Reading the code, you see repeated strings and repeated conditional structure; this increases the chance of inconsistent changes. Later, if the Gold tier multiplier changes from fifteen to twenty percent and you forget to update one method, the system becomes inconsistent. That is the exact maintenance risk Extract Method aims to remove. Not all duplicated code is identical. Often the shared block varies in small ways—for instance, the printed message or whether a caller needs a points multiplier or a discount rate. Parameterization is the act of identifying those varying parts and turning them into arguments for the extracted method. This keeps a single implementation while allowing flexible behavior. A concrete example: if two call sites differ only by the message context, pass a context parameter or a formatting string to the helper. A common trap is to let the helper reach into external variables instead of accepting parameters. That creates hidden dependencies and reduces reuse. Another pitfall is passing large object graphs instead of the specific values the helper needs; prefer explicit, minimal arguments. Use this checklist each time you plan an Extract Method refactor. First, confirm the block expresses a single responsibility. If you cannot name it in a short phrase, split the chunk. Second, verify the block repeats in multiple places or is complex enough that centralizing improves clarity. Third, design the method signature: list the exact values you must pass in as parameters. Fourth, choose a clear, intent-revealing name. Fifth, extract the method in a small change and run focused tests. Sixth, replace all original occurrences with calls to the new helper and re-run tests. Seventh, review for new dependencies and reduce them by passing explicit parameters. Eighth, update documentation or comments if the extracted logic clarifies business intent. Centralizing logic via Extract Method supports the Single Source of Truth principle: a piece of information or a business rule should exist in only one place. When you obey this principle, changes happen in one place, tests continue to pass, and you reduce the cognitive load for future maintainers. Imagine a billing rule scattered in five files. Updating that rule safely requires changing all five places and running many tests. Centralization reduces those five changes to one. A frequent misconception is that extracting into a helper moves complexity around instead of reducing it. The difference is intent and scope: a well-named helper clarifies what the rule does, while scattered copies force readers to re-derive intent each time. In larger systems, single-source helpers can also be reused by multiple modules and become the foundation for higher-level abstractions. The practical question is this: when does centralization add coupling that outweighs its benefits? Use tests, small-step refactoring, and code review to ensure the helper remains focused and loosely coupled. Let's summarize the three core concepts you should remember. First, duplicated code is repeated intent—identical or similar blocks implementing the same rule—and it increases maintenance cost and risk. Second, Extract Method centralizes repeated logic into a single, named method. Do it in small steps, pick clear names, and run tests after each change. Third, parameterization makes extracted methods flexible: pass differing values as arguments instead of relying on hidden state. Keep method signatures small and focused.
